summary: The Global activity threat map on the overview. Land is painted on a canvas from the bit mask generated by scripts/build_world_dots.py (decoded once, scaled for devicePixelRatio, batched with Path2D and tinted near risky cities), while an SVG overlay holds city markers, curved travel arcs in three categories, comets on impossible-travel arcs and live pings. overview.js creates it with the `geo` data from the dashboard API and forwards every live event to its `ping()` method.

notes.text: Header comment. The map has two layers: land is a canvas of about 3,800 dots decoded from a 3.6 KB bit mask, and cities, travel arcs and live pings are an SVG overlay. Both use the equirectangular projection, where longitude and latitude map linearly to x and y.
Imports escaping, formatting and `raw` from dom.js, plus the motion helpers, including `drawIn` for arcs and `motionPath` for comets.
Imports the generated land mask `WORLD`, the shared tooltip, and `LEVEL_COLORS`/`cssVar`, which turn CSS colour tokens into real colour strings the canvas can use.

`LAND` is computed once, when the module loads (an immediately-invoked function), so the mask is decoded a single time however often the map redraws. `cells` collects the `[col, row]` grid position of every land dot.

Each mask row is a hex string in which every digit encodes 4 cells: `parseInt(h, 16)` gives 0–15, `toString(2)` writes it in binary and `padStart(4, "0")` restores leading zeros (3 becomes 0011). Joined, a 45-digit row becomes 180 characters of 0s and 1s, one per 2° column.
Walks the row's bits and records a land cell wherever the bit is 1; the closing line ends the row callback.
Returns the list (3,791 cells with the current mask) and runs the function immediately.
The SVG namespace URI. SVG elements created from JavaScript must use `createElementNS` with it; `createElement("path")` would make an unknown HTML element that never renders.
The most travel arcs shown at once, which keeps the map readable and the DOM small.

`worldMap(el, geo, { onCity })`. `geo` comes from the API (`geo_overview` in iip/queries.py) with `cities` and recent `arcs`, and `onCity` is a click callback the overview uses to open the events list filtered to that city.
Adds the `worldmap` class, whose CSS makes the container `position: relative` so the canvas and SVG can be stacked exactly on top of each other.
Creates the two layers: a canvas for the land (hidden from screen readers, since it is decoration) and an SVG overlay with `role="img"` and a label.
Keeps references to both layers.

State shared by the inner functions: width `W` and height `H` in CSS pixels, `cell` (pixels per grid cell), `data` (the `geo` object) and `revealed`, which becomes true once the intro animation has finished.
Resolves the four risk colours once; canvas `fillStyle` needs real colour strings, not `var()`.

The projection. Equirectangular means longitude and latitude map linearly to x and y: x is the longitude's position across the 360° span, and y is the latitude's distance down from the top edge (82°N) across the cropped 140° span (82°N to 58°S), each scaled to pixels.
`drawDots(progress)` paints the land; `progress` (0–1) is how far the reveal has swept across, defaulting to 1 (everything).

`devicePixelRatio` scaling: on a high-density screen (ratio 2) the canvas holds twice as many pixels per side as CSS pixels (set up in `layout`), and `setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0)` scales all drawing so the code can work in CSS pixels while the result stays crisp. `setTransform` replaces the transform rather than multiplying it, so repeated calls never compound.
Clears the previous frame; during the reveal this function runs on every animation frame.
`front` is the x of the reveal's leading edge. It travels to `W + 60`, so by the end the edge and its scan line have moved fully off the right side.
The hot cities: those whose peak risk is 60 or more (HIGH or CRITICAL), with their projected pixel position and level colour. Land near them gets tinted.
`reach` is how far the tint spreads (4.2 grid cells) and `radius` the dot size (27% of a cell, never below 0.9 px); both scale with the map's width.
`base` is one `Path2D` that will hold every ordinary dot, and `tinted` collects the dots near hot cities, which need their own colours.
For each land cell, computes the centre of its grid square in pixels and skips it if the reveal hasn't reached it yet.
`best` will hold the nearest hot city found so far; `null` means none in range.
Checks every hot city: `Math.hypot` gives the straight-line pixel distance, and a city becomes `best` if it is within `reach` and closer than the current best. The closing brace ends the inner loop.
**Risk heat tint**: a dot near a hot city takes that city's colour, with an opacity that falls linearly from 0.87 at the city to 0.12 at the edge of `reach`, so risky places glow softly.

Otherwise the dot joins the shared path. `moveTo` jumps to the circle's starting point first; without it, `arc` would draw a straight line from the previous dot and every dot would merge into one shape. The closing brace ends the loop.

**Path2D batching**: all the ordinary dots (up to about 3,800 circles) are filled with one call, in 15% white. One fill is far cheaper than thousands of separate draw calls, which matters because the reveal redraws every frame.
Tinted dots differ in colour and opacity, so they are drawn one by one; `globalAlpha` sets the opacity of the next fill.
Each tinted dot is its own circle, 15% larger than a normal dot so the heat stands out. The closing brace ends the loop.
Restores full opacity so later drawing isn't faded.
While the reveal is running, draws the **scan line**: a 40 px gradient from transparent to 35% aqua (the accent colour, which marks live activity, not risk) at the leading edge.
Fills a full-height 40 px strip just behind the front with that gradient, so a glowing bar seems to sweep across the world. The closing brace ends the `if`.
Closes `drawDots`.
`arcPath(a, b)` returns the SVG path for a trip between two places, starting by projecting both ends to pixels.
`lift` sets how far the curve's control point is raised: 28% of the straight-line distance between the ends, capped at 90 px, so longer trips arc higher, like flight paths.

A **quadratic Bézier** (`Q`) with one control point, placed horizontally halfway between the ends and `lift` pixels above the higher end (smaller y is higher in SVG), so the curve bows upward and peaks about halfway towards that control point. Coordinates are rounded to one decimal to keep the path short.

Sorts an arc into one of three categories: `impossible` (the engine flagged impossible travel), `hostile` (the move was deliberately not judged, `assessed: false`, because the event failed or came from a flagged IP; the legend calls this an unverified origin) or else `plausible`. The strict `=== false` means an arc without an `assessed` field counts as plausible.
`arcNode(arc)` builds one SVG `path` element, created in the SVG namespace.
Sets its curve and its class: `arc plausible`, `arc hostile` or `arc impossible`, which charts.css styles as slate, dashed orange, or red with a glow.

Packs the tooltip data (route, distance, speed and category, separated by `|`) into a `data-tip` attribute so the hover handler needs no lookup; an unknown distance or speed (null from the backend) becomes `?`.
Returns the path; the closing brace ends `arcNode`.
`layout(animateIn)` sizes both layers and rebuilds the overlay; it runs on first show and on every width change, starting from the container's width.

The height keeps the grid's aspect ratio (180 columns by 70 rows), and `cell` is one 2° grid square in pixels. Both axes use 2° steps, so the cells are square and the dot grid lines up with `project()`.
Sets the container's height explicitly, because both layers are absolutely positioned and would otherwise give it no height.
The canvas's backing store is sized in device pixels (`W × dpr` by `H × dpr`); setting `canvas.width` also clears the canvas and resets its drawing state.
The canvas's CSS size stays `W × H`, so a high-density screen packs twice the pixels into the same space; together with `setTransform` in `drawDots` that gives sharp dots.
The SVG's `viewBox` matches the canvas's CSS size, so one SVG unit equals one CSS pixel and `project()` produces the same coordinates for both layers.
Comment introducing the arc selection.
`seen` is a Set of the route keys already kept.

Removes duplicate routes, keyed by origin, destination and category: `!seen.has(key) && seen.add(key)` keeps only the first occurrence (`Set.add` returns the set, which is truthy). The API sends arcs newest first, so each route keeps its most recent trip, and only the first 36 survive.
Comment introducing the label placement.
`placed` remembers the positions of labels already accepted.
Sorts a copy of the cities by event count (busiest first) and projects each one.

**Label collision avoidance**: a city is skipped once six labels exist, or when its label would land within 64 px horizontally and 14 px vertically of one already placed (roughly a label's width and height), so labels never overprint each other.
Otherwise its position is recorded and it is kept; the result is the list of names to label.
Rebuilds the overlay as four layers in paint order: arcs at the bottom, then comets, then cities, with pings on top. Each city is mapped to markup.

Projects the city and sizes its dot logarithmically: 2.4 px plus 0.45 × log2(1 + events), capped at 5.5 px, so busy hubs are bigger without dwarfing quieter cities (the +1 keeps a city with no events at the 2.4 px minimum).
Cities that reached HIGH or CRITICAL get a `pulse` ring that a CSS animation scales up and fades out, forever.
Labelled cities show their name up to the first comma (London, UK becomes London), escaped and placed just right of the dot.

Each city is a group carrying its level class (for colour) and its name in `data-name`. Inside: the pulse, an invisible circle of radius 10 that enlarges the hover and click target, the visible dot, and the label.
Joins the city markup and closes the layers with the empty pings group.
Appends the arc paths oldest first (a reversed copy of the newest-first list), so the newest paint on top; `slice()` copies first because `reverse()` mutates in place.

The intro runs only on the first layout with motion enabled. A `{ p }` object is tweened from 0 to 1 over 1.6 s and each frame calls `drawDots(p)`, producing the **scan-line reveal**; when it completes, `revealed` becomes true so live arcs may be added.

Cities pop in: they fade in and scale up from 20% with a springy `outBack` overshoot, 35 ms apart from 500 ms. charts.css sets `transform-box: fill-box` and `transform-origin: center`, so each one scales around its own centre.
Plausible and impossible arcs draw themselves along their length from 900 ms, 45 ms apart.
Hostile arcs fade in instead, because `drawIn` works by rewriting a stroke's dash pattern, which would wipe out their dashed style.
Without the intro (a resize, motion turned off, or a hidden tab), the land is drawn complete and the map counts as revealed straight away.
Starts the comets after either branch; the closing brace ends `layout`.

Comet flights loop forever, so their animations are kept in `comets` and `stopComets()` cancels them. A relayout on resize replaces the SVG; without cancelling, the old comets kept animating detached elements forever (anime.js doesn't notice), and every width change or overview visit added three more. `cancel?.()` is optional-chained because `animate` returns a plain promise when anime.js is unavailable.
`startComets` puts moving dots on impossible-travel arcs, first stopping any previous flights.
It does nothing if the overlay hasn't been built or motion is off, since motion.js would jump the animation to its end and leave each comet as a static dot at the end of its arc.
Picks the last three impossible arcs in the DOM, which are the three most recent because arcs are appended oldest first.
Each comet is a small SVG circle with class `comet` (white with a red glow in charts.css), added to the comets layer.

`motionPath(path)` wraps anime.js's `svg.createMotionPath`, which returns `translateX`, `translateY` and `rotate` values that follow the arc's shape; spreading them into `animate` makes the comet fly along the arc. Each flight takes 2.6 s, the first starts after 1.8 s and each later comet 0.7 s after the previous one, looping forever with a 0.9 s pause. The animation is kept in `comets` so it can be cancelled.
Closes the loop and `startComets`.
One `pointermove` listener on the SVG serves every city and arc (event delegation). It is attached once, outside `layout`, because the SVG element survives re-layouts; only its contents are replaced.
Finds whether the pointer is over a city group or an arc.
For a city, looks up its data by the name stored in `data-name`.
Tooltip: the city's name, its event count, its peak risk in that level's colour and, if any customers live there, how many.
For an arc, unpacks the four fields stored in `data-tip`.

Turns the category into the verdict shown as the tooltip's title. Unjudged arcs say why they weren't judged: the event came from a flagged IP or was a failed sign-in, both cases where geolocation can't be trusted.
Tooltip: the verdict, the route, the distance and the implied speed (`+km` turns the text back into a number for formatting), or `?` when unknown.
Over neither, the tooltip is hidden; the last line closes the handler.
Hides the tooltip when the pointer leaves the map.
Clicking a city calls `onCity` with its name, if a callback was given.

Comment explaining the start-up: lay out immediately (reading `clientWidth` forces the browser to compute layout, even in a background tab), then again on resize, because a ResizeObserver alone waits for a rendering step that hidden tabs never run.
`check` mirrors `responsive` in charts/core.js: it measures the width in whole pixels and does nothing if it is 0 or unchanged.
`first` is true only before the first layout, so the intro plays once; then `check` records the width and calls `layout`.
Observes size changes and calls `check` right away.
Returns the map's public API. `destroy` disconnects the observer and cancels the comet flights; the overview registers it to run when the page is left.
`ping(event)` is called by the overview for every event pushed over the Server-Sent Events stream: it ripples at the event's city and draws its travel arc if the customer moved.
Finds the event's city and gives up if it isn't on the map or the map hasn't been laid out yet (`W` is still 0).
Projects the city and creates a ring circle in the SVG namespace.
Places the ring at the city with a 3 px radius and the event's level class, which colours its stroke.
Adds it to the pings layer; the `?.` skips this if the overlay isn't there.

**Live ping**: the ring expands (to 30 px for HIGH and CRITICAL events, 16 px otherwise) while fading out over 1.6 s, then removes itself. anime.js animations are thenable, and `then?.()` only calls `then` if the returned value has one.
With motion off the ring is removed at once, so no static circle is left behind.
If the event carries travel context, looks up the city the customer came from.

Only once the intro has finished (`revealed`) and the origin is on the map, builds an arc object in the shape `arcNode` expects: the spread copies the trip's fields (including `assessed` and `impossible`) and the from/to names are swapped for full city objects with coordinates.
Creates the arc and appends it last, so it paints on top as the newest.
Dashed hostile arcs fade in; the others draw themselves along their path.
If there are now more than 36 arcs, removes the first one in the DOM, which is the oldest. The closing brace ends the `if`.
Closes `ping`, the returned object and `worldMap`.
`MAP_LEGEND` returns the legend's HTML wrapped in `raw`, so the overview's `html` template inserts it without escaping.

One sample line per arc category, styled by charts.css to match the map: slate for plausible travel, dashed orange for an unverified origin (a flagged IP or failed sign-in, so the trip wasn't judged) and red for impossible travel.
A dot in the resolved CRITICAL colour labelled as a risky city, then the closing tag of the legend.
